records.question: Where does each FORTRESS America base project stand on the proof ladder?
records.answer: Of the 10 base projects the FORTRESS registry tracks, only MCAS Miramar microgrid has a public island test; 4 have public operating descriptions with different boundaries, 4 are at selection or negotiation, 1 is a prototype, and FORTRESS itself has no published site list, definition or funding yet.

records.question: MKUltra: what did the June 30, 2026 hearing establish, and what is still open?
records.answer: On June 30, 2026 the House Oversight Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets (chair Rep. Anna Paulina Luna) heard Stephen Kinzer (book: Poisoner in Chief), Tom O'Neill (book: Chaos), Dr. Elizabeth Ginexi (former NIH) on MKUltra. It is a declassification and oversight hearing, not a prosecution, and made no legal finding. The chair committed on the record to contact the German government about Camp King and Villa Schuster. All 5 follow-ups have no recorded status since June 30, 2026, and only 1 of 5 cited sources is primary.

records.question: The rules: who is allowed to do what, and is it law yet?
records.answer: This page reads every rule the library holds on U.S. crypto in one walk: the GENIUS Act (enacted July 18, 2025) and its 28 dated steps, 14 of them proposals not yet final; the 8 other crypto rules, orders and bills and where each stands; the Crypto Hub's nine-step legal process walk with its 7 worked cases and qualification records; the SEC's custody proposal provision by provision (36 provisions, all 760 pages and 342 comment questions); the CFTC's 30-provision baseline; the SEC's Innovation Exemption (12 conditions, 15 clocks); the Federal Reserve Board's two GENIUS proposals; and 9 other jurisdictions' laws. A proposal grants no permission to anyone until it is final.

records.question: The money: what is the dollar on the chain, who owes it, and what backs it?
records.answer: This page reads every crypto dollar the library tracks: 36 coins and tokens (17 of them payment stablecoins or candidates), each with its exact issuing company, legal route, reserves and who holds them, attestation, redemption terms, size, freeze power (33 can freeze) and yield; then the July card decks that first mapped issuers, DeFi dollars, company control and GENIUS events; the Crypto Hub's 54 cash-leg nodes, which separate a stablecoin from a bank deposit and from central-bank money; and the dated filings and central-bank digital money moves. Who owes the dollar is always a named legal entity, not a brand or a chain.

records.question: The records: which record controls title, and what gets booked
records.answer: This page follows the record, not the token: who books what, and whose record decides who owns it. It opens with the 3 process walks of how a trade, a payment and a fund subscription work today, and the debit-and-credit entries each party books at every step; then the steps-and-rights walks and transaction maps; the 17 asset traces (USDC from mint to redemption, BUIDL and others); the 7 accounting layers; the current U.S. stack; Securitize's 4 record models; DTC's records; the SEC transfer agent proposal; and 61 dated tokenization and clearing filings. A token, a chain or a software vendor books nothing by itself; only an entity whose own books hold the asset or the claim does.

records.question: The operators: which companies and networks run it, and how far along is each?
records.answer: This page reads every operator the library tracks and how far along each one is, in one status vocabulary: 16 banks and asset managers across seven capabilities with where the proof stops, 32 card and processor products, 12 market systems, the money-machine seats; the bank transition, corporate stack and stack expansion comparisons; the Crypto Hub's 23 families with all 302 nodes and 372 connections; the field guide, the build-out ledger and the 112 vetted October 19 updates; and the 220 named actors and every placement. Announced is not live, and a partnership is not control.

records.question: The access: who may touch the Fed, and who holds a charter or license?
records.answer: This page reads every gate between crypto firms and the dollar system: the 36 institutions in the Fed-account and bank-charter queue, firm by firm (2 with a full master account, 1 with a limited account, 1 waiting, 1 in court); the 4 account types and what each allows; the queue counts; the 59-entry dated charter record; the legal routes map (26 jobs, 52 routes, 57 firms and public bodies); the 14 transition gates; the court cases on Fed accounts and on removing a Fed governor; and every legal placement. A charter and a Fed account are separate decisions by different agencies.

records.question: The settlement: where does the cash finally settle, and in what kind of money?
records.answer: In most of what the library holds, the cash still settles in money that already existed. Swift's ledger coordinates commitments among 17 listed banks, 8 of which have a completed pairing located; final settlement happens afterwards through existing payment systems. Of the 12 market systems, 1 settles in central-bank money by the master's own description (Sterling Fnality Payment System), 4 move banks' own tokenized deposits, and for 7 the master does not say. Who finances the interval before settlement: banks validated funding and managed the interval before external settlement. Customer availability can precede bank cash receipt.

records.question: Failure and remedy: when it breaks, who can freeze, who pays, who decides?
records.answer: For 18 of the 36 crypto dollars the library tracks, the issuer can freeze or block coins; for 15 the terms read do not say. When a firm collapsed, customers were being paid back at least partly in 3 of the 10 cases on the International Crypto Map, and courts decided whether customer crypto was the customer's property or the estate's. The 7 programmable-payment failures were corrected by forks, freezes or restitution, not one rule. 37 of 41 U.S. jurisdictions in the register have enacted UCC Article 12, the law on who owns a controllable electronic record.
